title: ABSALOM WAITED TWO YEARS Before Taking Revenge for What Happened to Tamar
paragraphs: ABSALOM WAITED TWO YEARS Before Taking Revenge for What Happened to Tamar

He barely spoke about it. He did not explode that day. He waited. And for two years, something deadly was growing behind the silence. But the most heartbreaking person in 2 Samuel 13 may not be the man who took revenge—or even the man he killed. It is the woman whose cries everyone else eventually learned to live around.
There are Bible stories that comfort you.
And then there are Bible stories that corner you.
They make you uncomfortable because there is no polished hero standing in the middle of the chapter. No quick resolution. No beautiful ending before the page turns.
Just sin.
Silence.
A wounded woman.
An angry brother.
A father who hears what happened.
And two years later...
blood.
This is 2 Samuel 13.
And if you read it too quickly, you may think this is simply the story of Amnon, Tamar, and Absalom.
It isn't.

It is also a terrifying picture of what can happen when lust is disguised as love, when wounded people are left carrying devastation, when anger is allowed to become hatred, and when human beings decide that because justice has not arrived quickly enough, they will become justice themselves.
And somewhere inside this story...
you may recognize yourself.
Maybe not in Amnon's crime.
Maybe not in Absalom's murder.
But perhaps in the waiting.
The resentment.
The memory you keep replaying.
The wound you say you have forgiven but still secretly rehearse.
The person whose name can change your breathing.
The injustice nobody seemed to take seriously enough.
The prayer you prayed while wondering why God did not fix everything immediately.
Before we talk about Absalom's revenge, however, we need to remember something Scripture refuses to let us forget.
This story begins with Tamar.
Not Absalom.
Tamar.
She was a daughter of David and the sister of Absalom. Amnon, another son of David, became consumed with desire for her.
The Hebrew text initially uses the language:
וַיֶּאֱהָבֶהָ — vayye'ehaveha
"He loved her."
But what follows exposes the horrifying difference between biblical love and selfish desire wearing love's clothing.
Real love does not manipulate someone into isolation.
Real love does not ignore "no."
Real love does not overpower.
Real love does not use another person's body to satisfy itself.
Amnon called what he felt love.
His actions revealed something else.
Tamar pleaded with him.
She reasoned with him.
She resisted him.
Scripture does not portray her as consenting to what happened.
Yet Amnon refused to listen.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 13:14 says:
וְלֹא אָבָה לִשְׁמֹעַ בְּקוֹלָהּ
"He was unwilling to listen to her voice."
Then Scripture records that he overpowered and violated her.
There is something unbearably important in those words.
He would not listen to her voice.
Because sin has a way of making another person's humanity inconvenient.
Lust says, "What I want matters more than what this costs you."
Pride says, "What I feel matters more than what God commands."
Bitterness says, "What they deserve matters more than what hatred is doing to me."
Sin keeps turning down every other voice until only desire remains.
Then something chilling happened.
After Amnon violated Tamar, the "love" he claimed to have for her became intense hatred.
The woman he supposedly could not live without became the woman he wanted removed from his presence.
Because she had never been loved properly in the first place.
She had been desired.
There is a difference.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that distinction.
You are not loving someone when you use them.
You are not loving someone when you manipulate them.
You are not loving someone when your affection requires them to violate God's commands.
You are not loving someone when their boundaries make you angry.
Biblical love does not consume another human being.
Biblical love seeks their good.
Tamar was thrown out.
The door was shut behind her.
And Scripture gives us one of the most haunting images in the chapter.
She put ashes on her head.
She tore the special garment she wore.
She placed her hand upon her head.
And she walked away crying aloud.
Not quietly.
Not invisibly.
Crying.
The Hebrew says:
הָלוֹךְ וְזָעָקָה — halokh weza'aqah
She went away crying out.
Do not rush past her cry just because you already know what Absalom eventually does.
Sit there for a moment.
A woman walked out of that house carrying something she never asked for.
Something had been done to her.
Her grief was not evidence that she was dirty.
Her devastation did not make her guilty of Amnon's sin.
The shame belonged to the one who violated her.
And perhaps this is where this ancient chapter suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because there are still Tamars.
People carrying wounds created by somebody else's sin.
People smiling in photographs while privately trying to understand what happened to them.
People sitting in churches while fighting memories nobody around them knows exist.
People who have spent years wondering whether God sees the room nobody else saw.
He does.
God does not confuse the wounded with the one who wounded them.
He does not need darkness to become light before He can see what happened there.
Then Tamar encountered Absalom.
He realized what had happened.
And Tamar remained in his house.
The Hebrew describes her with a devastating word:
שֹׁמֵמָה — shomemah
It carries the sense of being devastated, desolate, ruined, or left appalled.
The chapter does not give us some sentimental sentence saying everything quickly became normal again.
It simply leaves Tamar there.
Desolate.
And then David heard.
Scripture says King David became extremely angry.
But the chapter records no immediate punishment of Amnon by David.

We should be careful here. The Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 13:21 explicitly tells us David was very angry; some ancient textual witnesses add an explanation for why David did not rebuke Amnon, but that additional wording is not present in the standard Hebrew Masoretic text. So we should not pretend Scripture tells us more than it actually does.
What the narrative undeniably shows is that Absalom's hatred began burning.
Second Samuel 13:22 says Absalom would not speak to Amnon either good or bad.
Then Scripture tells us why.
He hated Amnon because Amnon had violated Tamar.
Absalom's anger did not arise from an imaginary offense.
Something genuinely evil had happened.
That distinction matters.
The Bible does not require us to call evil good in order to forgive.
Forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened.
Forgiveness is not calling abuse acceptable.
Forgiveness does not mean protecting an offender from appropriate consequences.
And forgiveness certainly does not mean telling wounded people that justice does not matter.
God cares about justice.
But there is a dangerous place where righteous anger can mutate into something else.
And Absalom went there.
Then comes one of the coldest transitions in the chapter.
וַיְהִי לִשְׁנָתַיִם יָמִים
"After two full years..."
Two years.
Let that settle.
Approximately 730 days.
Seasons changed.
Meals were eaten.
Conversations happened.
Life apparently moved forward.
But hatred was still alive.
Absalom did not kill Amnon the next morning in an uncontrollable explosion.
He waited.
He planned.
He arranged a sheep-shearing celebration.
He invited the king's sons.
He specifically pressed for Amnon to attend.
And he instructed his servants to watch until Amnon's heart was merry with wine.
Then came the command.
Strike him.
Kill him.
Two years of silence ended in seconds of violence.
And here is where this story reaches through thousands of years and grabs us.
Because not every revenge story ends with literal blood.
Sometimes revenge looks like refusing to speak to someone for years.
Sometimes it looks like destroying their reputation.
Sometimes it looks like secretly celebrating their failure.
Sometimes it looks like making sure everyone knows what they did.
Sometimes it looks like repeatedly reopening the case in your mind, prosecuting them again, sentencing them again, punishing them again.
Sometimes nobody around you knows you are angry anymore.
You go to work.
You raise your children.
You worship.
You post Scripture.
You say, "I'm okay."
But somewhere inside your soul...
it is still day one.
Absalom waited two years.
And time alone did not heal him.
That should destroy one of our favorite clichés.
Time does not automatically heal every wound.
Sometimes time simply gives bitterness deeper roots.
Healing requires something more than passing days.
Some wounds need grief.
Some need truth.
Some need appropriate justice.
Some need wise counsel.
Some need boundaries.
Some need patient restoration.
But every human heart ultimately needs God.
Because you can move thousands of miles away and still carry someone inside your anger.
You can block their number while keeping their memory permanently unblocked in your mind.
You can stop talking about what happened and still allow what happened to determine who you are becoming.
And that is where Absalom's story becomes frightening.
The original injustice against Tamar was real.
But Absalom's response created another evil.
Amnon's sin did not make Absalom's murder righteous.
One person's wickedness does not give another person permission to become wicked in response.
Scripture later gives the principle plainly:
"Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord" (Romans 12:19).
That does not mean earthly authorities should ignore crime or that victims should remain in danger. Romans 13 immediately speaks about governing authority bearing responsibility against wrongdoing.
It means personal vengeance belongs in hands far more righteous than ours.
God can judge without becoming corrupted by hatred.
We cannot.
And maybe that is why this chapter hurts so badly.
Everybody seems to be losing something.
Tamar loses the life she knew.
Amnon is consumed by corrupt desire and later killed.
Absalom allows hatred to mature into murder and eventually enters a much larger rebellion that will tear David's household and kingdom apart.
David's family is fracturing before his eyes.
Sin never keeps its promises.
It always charges more than the advertisement said.
And this is exactly why we need more than moral improvement.
We need a Savior.
Because somewhere inside humanity's long history of lust, violence, shame, betrayal, silence, revenge, and broken families...
Jesus Christ entered.
Not as another wounded sinner looking for someone to punish.
Not as another powerful man exploiting vulnerable people.
But as the sinless Son of God.
Jesus does not minimize evil.
The cross itself proves how seriously God takes sin.
Grace is not God shrugging His shoulders at wickedness.
Grace is unimaginably costly.
At Calvary, Jesus bore sin's judgment so guilty people could be reconciled to God through faith in Him.
And that means the Gospel speaks to every person standing somewhere inside 2 Samuel 13.
To the wounded:
Jesus sees you.
To the ashamed:
what someone did to you does not put their guilt upon your soul.
To the bitter:
Jesus is not asking you to pretend the wound was imaginary. He is calling you to surrender vengeance before vengeance reshapes you.
To the person who has committed terrible sin:
repentance is still possible.
Do not hide behind excuses.
Do not rename lust "love."
Do not rename hatred "justice."
Do not rename pride "strength."
Bring the truth into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Run to Christ.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that sin doesn't matter.
The scandal is that Christ's grace can reach sinners who finally stop defending their darkness and come to Him empty-handed.
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23).
And yet sinners can be "justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" (Romans 3:24).
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that transforms.
Grace that refuses to leave you where it found you.
Maybe your two years have actually been twenty.
Maybe someone betrayed you and never apologized.
Maybe your father failed you.
Maybe your mother wounded you.
Maybe somebody abused your trust.
Maybe the person who damaged you appears to be living happily while you are still collecting pieces.
You do not need to pretend that doesn't hurt.
But please hear this:
Do not give the person who wounded you permission to keep shaping the person you are becoming.
Bring the wound to Jesus.
Again, if necessary.
And again.
Forgiveness can involve a real process of surrender. Reconciliation and restored trust are separate questions and can require repentance, wisdom, safety, and changed behavior.
But vengeance?
Give it to God.
Because hatred promises power while quietly building a prison.
Absalom thought killing Amnon would settle something.
But 2 Samuel does not end at chapter 13.
More grief was coming.
More separation.
More rebellion.
More death.
Unhealed sin keeps writing sequels.
But Jesus writes another kind of story.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored Peter.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed Paul into a servant of the Gospel.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, yet he turned toward Christ and received mercy.
This is what Jesus does.
He enters stories human beings would throw away.
He confronts sin without denying grace.
He gives mercy without calling evil good.
He receives repentant sinners without pretending repentance is unnecessary.
He takes people whose stories seem permanently defined by scandal...
and begins writing grace.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe you thought this article would only be about Absalom waiting two years.
But perhaps God has put His finger on something you have been carrying much longer.
A name.
A memory.
A secret.
A hatred.
A shame.
A sin you keep defending.
A wound you keep hiding.
Be honest before God.
What has been growing inside you while everybody thought you were fine?
You don't have to tell the whole internet your private story.
But do not lie to Jesus about it.
He already knows.
And He is still calling you.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only one fighting.
Someone may pray because you were brave enough to ask.
Someone may see your testimony and realize that Jesus still restores people.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns God's favor. It does not.
It cannot.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him, and salvation is God's gift of grace—not something bought by supporting a ministry.
But if this message helped you see Scripture more clearly, sharing it can place biblical truth in front of someone who may desperately need it.
Send it to the believer who has become bitter.
Send it to someone who needs to know that what happened to them does not have to become the final sentence of their life.
It is practical support for the work of creating and distributing Gospel-centered resources.
God does not need our money.
We need His mercy.
The greatest response you can make to this message is not clicking a button.
It is surrendering your heart.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ is calling you to release vengeance.
Seek help where you have been wounded.
Speak truth where silence has protected darkness.
Give appropriate justice to the authorities God has appointed.
And bring the parts nobody else sees to Jesus.
Because Tamar's cry reminds us that wounds are real.
Amnon's sin reminds us that desire without holiness can become destructive.
David's grief reminds us that anger alone does not repair what evil has broken.
Absalom's two-year wait reminds us that silence is not always healing.
And the Gospel reminds us that our worst chapter does not have to become our final chapter.
Jesus Christ walked toward a cross carrying sins He never committed.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And because the grave could not keep Him, sin does not get unquestioned ownership of the ending either.
So before you leave this article, ask yourself one question:
What have I been carrying for two years—or twenty—that Jesus is asking me to finally place into His hands?
Do not wait until bitterness writes another chapter.
Do not wait until secret sin becomes public destruction.
Do not wait until shame convinces you that grace has forgotten your address.
Come to Christ.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
There is grace for the guilty.
There is refuge for the wounded.
There is freedom from vengeance.
There is a new life for those who belong to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most frightening thing about Absalom's story was not simply that he waited two years.
It was that during those two years, the wound was still writing him—and Jesus is calling you to stop letting your wound hold the pen.
